metaDescription: Five hammer drills under $200, from a corded 7.5 amp unit to brushless DEWALT bare tools and SDS-Plus rotary hammers, with the tradeoffs spelled out.
expertTake: The ENEACRO 13 amp SDS-Plus is the pick if you actually have concrete to drill, because a piston-driven rotary hammer beats any clutch-type hammer drill in masonry. The DEWALT DCD806B is the cordless choice, but it is a bare tool, so the battery you already own decides its value. Skip a conventional hammer drill entirely if you only drill a few anchors a year, because a plain drill with a masonry bit and patience gets you there.
introParagraphs: A hammer drill adds a pulsing blow to the spinning bit so it can chip its way into brick, block and concrete. The label covers two very different mechanisms, and the amp, joule and blows-per-minute numbers on the box do not translate into the same real-world speed.

This guide explains what a spending cap of $200 buys, what you give up compared with a pro rotary hammer, and which figures are worth trusting. Our top picks are above and the reviews follow below. Prices move, and the cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: ENEACRO ENRH3201 13 Amp 1-1/4 in SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer
products.description:
The ENEACRO is a true rotary hammer, which means a piston inside the tool drives a striker that taps the back of an SDS-Plus bit. Because the bit slides freely in the chuck, the blow reaches the concrete without having to push against your arm, which is why it outperforms a clutch-type hammer drill in masonry. The 13 amp motor and 5.5 foot-pounds of impact energy put it in the range that drills 1/2 to 3/4 inch anchor holes without a fight.

It has four functions, including drill-only mode for wood and steel and a chisel mode, and a safety clutch that slips if the bit binds. The tradeoff is size and cost of bits: SDS-Plus bits are a separate purchase, and the tool is heavier than the Hammerhead or Seesii. Against the DEKOPRO's 12.5 amp rating, the ENEACRO is a near twin, though its impact figure is quoted in foot-pounds while the DEKOPRO quotes joules, and 5.5 J is the stronger blow. Compared with the corded Hammerhead, it is the tool that actually earns the hammer label in poured concrete.

Expect to buy a set of SDS-Plus bits and a pair of safety glasses. Clean the chuck dust boot, grease it per the manual and keep an eye on carbon brushes after a few years of regular concrete work.
products.bestFor: Anyone drilling concrete anchors, tapcons and masonry holes regularly.
pros: Piston-driven hammering beats clutch-type drills in concrete
13 amp motor and 5.5 ft-lbs of impact energy handle anchors
Four functions including chisel mode and drill-only
Safety clutch protects wrists if the bit binds
cons: Heavier than a standard hammer drill and needs SDS bits
Corded only, so you need an outlet or an extension
Chuck dust boot and brushes need periodic attention

products.name: DEKOPRO 12.5 Amp 1-1/4 in SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer Drill
products.description:
The DEKOPRO is a 12.5 amp SDS-Plus rotary hammer that lists 0 to 1000 rpm, 0 to 4600 blows per minute and 5.5 joules of impact energy. Joules measure the energy of each blow, and for a rotary hammer that is the figure that predicts concrete speed better than amps do. At 5.5 J it is in the same bracket as the ENEACRO.

Its listing says four functions and a side selector for switching modes, with a safety clutch for protection. The tradeoff versus the ENEACRO is a marginally lower amp rating and a less established brand. Compared with the Seesii, which is rated 3 J and 850 watts, the DEKOPRO hits roughly 80 percent harder per blow, which matters for bits above 1/2 inch.

Ownership is similar to the ENEACRO: buy SDS-Plus bits, keep the chuck greased and replace worn carbon brushes. Note that the 4600 BPM figure is a no-load figure, and the real rate under load is lower.
products.bestFor: Buyers wanting SDS-Plus performance at a lower outlay.
pros: 5.5 J impact energy is the strongest claim in the SDS-Plus group
Side selector switches between four functions quickly
Safety clutch limits kickback if the bit binds
Handles holes up to 1-1/4 inch in concrete
cons: No-load BPM figure drops under load
Lesser known brand with uncertain parts support
Needs a separate SDS-Plus bit set

products.name: Seesii 9 Amp 850W SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer, 3J
products.description:
The Seesii drops the impact energy to 3 joules and the motor to 9 amps, which makes it lighter and easier to handle on a ladder. The stated limits are about 1-1/32 inch in concrete, 1-3/16 inch in wood and 1/2 inch in metal, honest numbers that match what a tool this size can do. Its four modes include drill, hammer, chisel and Vario-Lock, which sets the chisel angle.

The tradeoff is power. Compared with the ENEACRO's 5.5 ft-lbs and the DEKOPRO's 5.5 J, the Seesii hits at roughly half the energy, so it is slower in concrete, and holes above 1/2 inch take longer. It does draw less current, so it is kinder to a long extension cord.

It is a good choice for installing shelves, cabinets and light fixtures on masonry. Keep the chuck clean, avoid forcing the tool and let it do the work, since a 3 J hammer does not reward pressure.
products.bestFor: Light masonry jobs such as shelves, fixtures and small anchors.
pros: Lighter body and 9 amp draw suit ladder work
Four modes including a Vario-Lock chisel angle setting
Stated limits for concrete, wood and metal are realistic
1300 rpm top speed drills wood and metal quickly
cons: 3 J impact is roughly half the SDS-Plus rivals here
Slower in concrete with holes above 1/2 inch
Small brand with limited parts support

products.name: DEWALT DCD806B 20V MAX XR Brushless Hammer Drill, Tool Only
products.description:
The DCD806B is a clutch-type hammer drill: two ridged discs inside the gearbox click against each other to make small blows as the chuck turns. It is lighter and more convenient than a rotary hammer but weaker in concrete. Its brushless motor and anti-rotation system, which senses sudden twisting and cuts power, make it a safer tool when a bit binds in a joist.

It is sold as a bare tool, which means you need a 20V battery and charger. If you already own DEWALT packs it is excellent value, but if you do not, the cost of a battery and charger changes the price comparison with the corded rotary hammers. Its compact XR body keeps it among the lighter drills in this lineup.

Use it for 3/16 to 3/8 inch masonry anchors in brick and block, and for general drilling in wood and steel. Keep the chuck clean and store the tool away from dust.
products.bestFor: DEWALT battery owners who need an occasional masonry anchor.
pros: Brushless motor gives longer run time per battery
Anti-rotation system cuts power if the bit binds
Lighter and handier than any corded rotary hammer
Doubles as an everyday drill with hammer mode when needed
cons: Sold as a bare tool with no battery or charger

Only worthwhile if you already own 20V packs

products.name: Hammerhead HAHD075 7.5 Amp 1/2 in Corded Hammer Drill
products.description:
The Hammerhead is the simplest hammer drill in the roundup, a corded 7.5 amp tool with a 1/2 inch metal keyless chuck and a switch between drill and hammer drill modes. Because it is corded, it avoids the battery question completely and delivers steady power for as long as you feed it.

The weakness is the hammer mechanism, a clutch-type design with small blows suited to drilling 1/4 to 3/8 inch holes in brick and block. Compared with the Seesii and the SDS-Plus tools, it is slower in concrete, and on dense poured concrete it can take minutes per hole. It is a good fit for an occasional job rather than a regular one.

Ownership is simple: use masonry bits with carbide tips, keep it clean, and replace the tool, not the parts, if the hammer mechanism wears out.
products.bestFor: Occasional masonry anchors at the lowest cost.
pros: Corded design avoids any battery cost or run time limit
1/2 inch metal keyless chuck grips standard bits
Switches between drill and hammer drill modes
Includes a bit set for first jobs
cons: Clutch-type blows are slow in poured concrete
Not suited to holes above 3/8 inch in masonry
Brand support and parts are limited

buyingCriteria.explanation: A rotary hammer uses a piston to strike the back of the bit, while a hammer drill uses ridged discs that click as the chuck turns. The piston delivers far more energy per blow, which is why a 5.5 J SDS-Plus tool drills concrete faster than a 7.5 amp clutch-type tool. In this roundup the ENEACRO, DEKOPRO and Seesii are rotary hammers, and the Hammerhead and DEWALT drills are clutch-type.

Joules measure the energy of each blow and predict concrete speed better than amps. The DEKOPRO claims 5.5 J, the ENEACRO claims 5.5 ft-lbs (roughly 7.5 J), and the Seesii claims 3 J, so check the unit before you compare. A buyer mistake is comparing amps across brands, since a 13 amp motor wastes some of its power as heat and a tidy 9 amp tool with an efficient mechanism can drill nearly as fast.

A corded hammer drill never runs out, and cordless tools run flat when the bit is deep in concrete. The DEWALT DCD806B is a bare tool, so the pack and charger are an extra. If you own no 20V batteries, a corded rotary hammer is better value.

SDS-Plus chucks let the bit slide so the piston can strike it, while keyed or keyless chucks grip the bit. The ENEACRO, DEKOPRO and Seesii use SDS-Plus, and the Hammerhead and DEWALT use 1/2 inch chucks. SDS bits cost more but drill faster and do not slip.

A big bit that jams can twist the tool out of your hands. The ENEACRO and DEKOPRO have a safety clutch, and the DEWALT DCD806B has an anti-rotation system that cuts power. Do not use a hammer tool without a side handle.

Drill-only mode lets the tool serve in wood and steel, and chisel mode allows light demolition. The ENEACRO, DEKOPRO and Seesii list four modes, with the Seesii adding Vario-Lock for chisel angle. If you will only drill, hammer-drill mode is enough.

specDecoder.meaning: Amps measure how much current the motor draws, not how hard it hits. A tool with a poor mechanism can draw many amps and still be slow.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ENEACRO's 13 amps and the Hammerhead's 7.5 amps do not give a 2-to-1 performance ratio.

specDecoder.meaning: Impact energy per blow in joules or foot-pounds, with one joule about 0.74 foot-pounds. It tells you how hard each strike hits, and it is the closest thing to a standard for rotary hammers.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ENEACRO quotes 5.5 ft-lbs and the DEKOPRO 5.5 J, which are not the same, since 5.5 ft-lbs is about 7.5 J, so convert before ranking them.

specDecoder.meaning: BPM counts blows at no load. Under load the rate drops, and a high BPM with low energy per blow is less effective than a lower rate with more energy.
specDecoder.watchFor: Seesii's 5500 BPM beats DEKOPRO's 4600 on paper, but the DEKOPRO hits harder.

specDecoder.meaning: SDS-Plus is a bit shank with slots that lock into the chuck while letting it slide. This sliding allows the piston to hit the bit directly.
specDecoder.watchFor: SDS-Plus is not the same as SDS-Max, which is for larger tools.

specDecoder.meaning: A brushless motor commutates electronically, which saves energy and runs cooler. It is used in the DEWALT bare tools.
specDecoder.watchFor: A brushless motor does not make a clutch-type hammer drill strong in concrete.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hammer mechanism
howWeEvaluated.description: We began with whether each tool uses a piston or a clutch, since that sets concrete performance. The ENEACRO, DEKOPRO and Seesii are rotary hammers, while the Hammerhead and DEWALT are clutch-type.

howWeEvaluated.title: Impact energy
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated energy per blow after converting everything to joules. The ENEACRO and DEKOPRO led, with the Seesii at 3 J, and clutch-type tools such as the Hammerhead and DEWALT do not publish joule figures at all, which tells you where they sit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered corded versus bare cordless tools. The DEWALT bare tools are only good value if you own the pack, since a battery and charger can add a large share to the real cost. Corded rotary hammers avoid that issue but require an outlet or a heavy extension cord.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at safety clutches and anti-rotation systems. The DEWALT DCD806B led with anti-rotation, followed by the safety clutches in the ENEACRO and DEKOPRO.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted recurring owner themes such as chuck slip, bit availability and parts. Lesser known brands scored cautiously on parts support.

cards.label: Rotary hammer
cards.text: The ENEACRO, DEKOPRO and Seesii use a piston to deliver energy per blow. They drill concrete much faster but need SDS bits and weigh more.

cards.label: Hammer drill
cards.text: The Hammerhead and DEWALT use a clutch. They accept standard bits and handle general drilling, but concrete takes longer.

howToChoose.note: Choose a rotary hammer if you drill concrete regularly. Choose a hammer drill if masonry is occasional.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: An SDS-Plus tool with at least 3 J, a depth stop and a side handle. Use carbide-tipped bits and clear dust from each hole.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ENEACRO and DEKOPRO suit 1/2 to 3/4 inch anchors. The Seesii suits smaller anchors, and the DEWALT DCD806B suits quick holes.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You drill concrete weekly. A branded SDS-Plus rotary hammer outlasts the ENEACRO and DEKOPRO, with better bits and service.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You drill a few holes a year. The Hammerhead HAHD075 or the Seesii does that work.

maintenance.why: SDS chucks pack with concrete dust. Grease keeps the bit sliding and the piston from wearing.

maintenance.interval: After several years of regular use
maintenance.why: Worn brushes cause weak power and sparking. Replace them in the corded rotary hammers.
A dull carbide tip slows the tool and overheats it. Replace bits that no longer cut.
Concrete dust clogs airflow and raises motor temperature. Blow out the vents with compressed air.
A nicked cord is a shock hazard. Replace damaged cords.

faq.q: Do I need a rotary hammer or a hammer drill?
faq.a: Use a rotary hammer for regular concrete work and a clutch-type hammer drill for occasional brick and block. A rotary hammer needs SDS bits.

faq.q: What does $200 buy in a hammer drill?
faq.a: A corded SDS-Plus rotary hammer or a clutch-type hammer drill. You give up brushless motors, pro-grade clutches and battery platforms. The cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

faq.q: Why is a DEWALT bare tool included?
faq.a: It falls under the cap as a bare tool, so you must supply a battery and charger. If you do not own them, the corded options give better value, and the cordless tools make sense mainly for existing DEWALT owners.

faq.q: Is joules or amps the better figure?
faq.a: Joules, because it measures energy per blow. Amps measure only current draw.

faq.q: Do I need eye and ear protection?
faq.a: Yes. Concrete chips and the noise of a hammer tool are hazards, so wear safety glasses, ear protection and a dust mask.

faq.q: Can I use the Seesii for larger holes?
faq.a: It can, but it is slow above 1/2 inch because it hits at about half the energy of the larger units. For larger holes choose the ENEACRO or DEKOPRO, which are built for 3/4 inch anchors and bigger.
